issues.description: Element: SealSaloon.stock (the shared stock attribute). The problem statement first instructs (lines 70-71) that SealSaloon should have a final Stock stock initialized in the constructor (implying an instance, final field initialized in the instance constructor). Elsewhere in the same problem statement (lines 77-81) it then requires that the stock attribute must be static (shared across all instances). The reference solution declares the field as static final (SealSaloon.java: line 5: private static final Stock stock = new Stock()). This contradiction (instance final initialized in constructor vs. static final initialized at declaration) will confuse students about whether to declare stock as an instance field initialized in the constructor or as a static field initialized at declaration/static initializer, and may cause tests or grading to fail depending on which interpretation students follow.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the design consistent in the problem statement and UML. Option A (recommended to match the solution): state that 'stock' is a shared static attribute (e.g., 'private static final Stock stock = new Stock();') and explain it should be initialized at the point of declaration or in a static initializer. Remove or modify the sentence that instructs students to initialize 'stock' in the instance constructor. Option B: if you want an instance final stock, change the 'Note' that requires stock to be static and update the reference solution and tests accordingly. Update the UML and all textual references accordingly so only one interpretation remains.

issues.description: Element: SealSaloon.checkOrderReady() method return type. The UML in the problem statement declares checkOrderReady() as returning void (+checkOrderReady(): void). The reference solution implements checkOrderReady() with a boolean return type (public boolean checkOrderReady() in SealSaloon.java). This mismatch in the specified method signature (void) vs. the actual reference implementation (boolean) can confuse students about the required signature and whether they must return a value; it may also lead to grading/test mismatches if tests expect one signature but student code implements the other.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the method signature consistent across artifacts. Either (A) change the problem statement/UML to specify checkOrderReady() returns boolean (and document what true/false means), or (B) change the reference solution to implement checkOrderReady() with a void return type (removing the boolean return) so it matches the UML and textual description. Update tests and examples accordingly.
